title: Priesthood of all believers
hook: Luther stressed that every baptized Christian has a priestly calling (1 Peter 2:9)

segments.voice: Yesterday, ordination: hands and prayer, setting people apart to serve. Your line was called to serve.

A cobbler bends over a shoe, stitching by lamplight. A blacksmith sweats at his forge. A farmer walks behind a plow. In Martin Luther's Germany, people spoke of a spiritual estate, the priests and monks, and a worldly estate, everyone else. Luther disagreed, loudly. In a letter to the German nobility, he wrote that the cobbler, the smith and the farmer each have the work of their trade, and yet all of them, by baptism, are alike consecrated priests. Not just the priest at the altar. The cobbler too. He found it in a much older letter.

That older letter is the first letter of Peter: "But ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people." Written to ordinary believers, not clergy. And Peter echoes a far older promise at Mount Sinai, where God tells Israel, "ye shall be unto me a kingdom of priests, and an holy nation." Jews read that verse as their own calling, and Peter's readers heard themselves invited into its language. So what does a priest do? A priest stands between: bringing people's needs to God, and God's blessing to people. Peter says this whole people exists to "shew forth the praises of him who hath called you out of darkness into his marvellous light." Luther pressed it hard. If every baptized person is a priest, no one stands higher before God because of their job. A pastor still serves, for good order, as we saw yesterday. But a mother changing diapers and a monk saying his prayers stand on the same ground. Protestant teachers built on it a high view of ordinary work as a calling. Other churches read the verse their own way. Catholic teaching speaks of a common priesthood shared by all the baptized, and a ministerial priesthood of the ordained, different in kind, yet ordered to one another. Orthodox Christians speak of the royal priesthood of the whole people of God, offering the world back to God in thanksgiving. And a line from Paul for any workbench: "whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men."
screen: `A ROYAL PRIESTHOOD, A HOLY NATION.` · `AN ECHO OF SINAI.` · `A PRIEST STANDS BETWEEN.` · `THE COBBLER ON THE SAME GROUND.` · then, large: `DO IT HEARTILY, AS TO THE LORD.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind the next task waiting for you, a shift, a report, a sink of dishes, an email you've been avoiding, and picture the people it touches. Picture doing it for them, carefully, as if it mattered beyond the paycheck. If you pray, offer the task to God before you start; if you don't, decide who it's really for, and hold that person in mind.
The priesthood of all believers. In this teaching, every baptized Christian is called to stand between God and the world, at the altar or the workbench.
Your line: a royal priesthood. At the altar, and at the cobbler's bench. Day one thousand ninety-nine.

howItsDone: Protestant churches teach the priesthood of all believers, often with a strong sense of ordinary work as a calling; Catholic teaching speaks of the common priesthood of the baptized alongside the ordained priesthood, and Orthodox Christians speak of the royal priesthood of the whole people of God.

original.note: Greek: a priesthood, a body of priests — the word in 1 Peter 2:9, "a royal priesthood."

what a scholar hears: 1 Peter 2:9 echoes Exodus 19:6. Luther pressed it in his letter to the German nobility; Catholic and Orthodox teaching read the verse their own way.

chat.says: Luther said a cobbler is a priest too? What did he mean by that?
options: That by baptism all are alike consecrated priests, so no job stands higher before God.
That cobblers should lead the Mass, since Luther wanted shoemakers to replace pastors.
That only craftsmen were priests, since Luther thought monks did no real work.
chat.meaning: In his letter to the German nobility, Luther wrote that the cobbler, the smith and the farmer are, by baptism, alike consecrated priests.

cobbler.meaning: a shoemaker, or someone who mends shoes

peculiar.meaning: in old English, belonging especially to someone

Mount Sinai.meaning: the mountain where, in Exodus, God speaks to Israel

ministerial priesthood.meaning: Catholic term for the priesthood of the ordained

notes: Luther paraphrase: in To the Christian Nobility he argues all the baptized are consecrated priests and that a cobbler, smith and farmer each have the work of their trade, yet all are alike consecrated priests and bishops. Confirm the wording of the paraphrase.
'A mother changing diapers and a monk saying his prayers stand on the same ground' is a modern illustration in Luther's spirit, not a Luther quotation. Confirm acceptable.
'Protestant teachers built on it a high view of ordinary work as a calling' is a historical characterization; confirm or soften.
Catholic summary paraphrases Lumen Gentium 10 (common and ministerial priesthood differ in essence and not only in degree); Orthodox summary is a characterization. Confirm fairness.
Exodus 19:6 framed as Israel's calling that Jews read as their own; Peter's use is not framed as replacing it. Confirm tone.
Original: ἱεράτευμα in 1 Peter 2:9; confirm pronunciation.
